extracted.intended_audience: working mathematicians, mathematics students, historians/philosophers of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A compact rubric for selecting problems and judging mathematical work according to von Neumann's aesthetic criteria: clarity of statement, genuine difficulty, a surprising core idea, explanatory principles, and architectural structure, plus connection to substantive motivation. Intended to guide both problem selection and assessment of proofs/results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem or result can be stated simply and concisely (often with everyday words, not jargon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann emphasizes that elegant mathematics is often expressible in a sentence or two intelligible to a non-specialist. A good test: can the result be communicated to a non-specialist in a sentence or two? Anti-pattern: highly technical, opaque formulations that obscure the basic point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of access
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is genuinely hard; standard or routine approaches fail to solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A valuable mathematical problem resists straightforward application of existing techniques. If the solution is merely an exercise in known machinery, it lacks the 'genuinely hard' quality von Neumann prizes. Scoring note: distinguish routine technical refinement from true obstacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprising twist (central idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The eventual solution turns on an unexpected idea — a reframing, a new connection, or an unanticipated tool — that suddenly makes the problem tractable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There should be a single striking insight one can quote in a sentence that captures why the problem yields. Von Neumann values surprise: an unforeseen move or perspective that unlocks the difficulty. Anti-pattern: lengthy work with no identifiable core idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying explanatory principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When deductions are long, there is some simple general principle that 'explains' the complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long calculations are acceptable only if an organizing principle ties them together. A calculation-heavy proof without an explanatory unifying idea is judged inelegant even if correct. Guidance: identify the principle that renders the calculations natural; if none exists, downgrade aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural / structural makeup
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof has a discernible architecture — a global plan rather than merely a sequence of local moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann insists on structure: a reader should be able to 'redraw the proof from a sketch' because of its overarching design. Scoring guidance: reward proofs with clear modular structure, strategic lemmas, and an intelligible flow; penalize proofs that are ad hoc chains of computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expositability to non-specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: The result and its key idea can be explained to non-specialists in an accessible way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to ease of statement but focused on exposition: a single-sentence articulation of the driving idea is evidence of elegance. Use this as a practical criterion for communicating significance beyond narrow specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to substantive motivation (empirical contact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work connects to substantive motivations — physical, computational, or other domains — rather than being purely internal to mathematical fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann warns that fields severed from empirical/scientific problems risk 'baroque' degeneration (art for art's sake). Periodic re-injection of empirical problems restores taste. Reward work that ties to applications or cross-domain motivation; view isolated technicality with suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth in scope or depth (not mere technical sophistication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy research program exhibits growth in scope or conceptual depth rather than only increasing technical sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: a program characterized solely by accumulating technical refinements without expanding its explanatory reach. Use this criterion to evaluate programs and trends as well as individual results: prefer developments that broaden understanding or open new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic evaluation summary: economy, surprise, structure, depth, connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical work should be judged by the same evaluative apparatus used for creative arts: economy, surprise, structure, depth, and connection to lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann's concluding synthesis encourages treating mathematical selection like artistic judgment. Apply these five lenses together — economical formulation, unexpected insight, architectural harmony, conceptual depth, and substantive connection — when forming an overall aesthetic assessment.
